title: The Thirteenth Figure
author: Lantern Original
summaryTr: Kerem, kasabadaki bir balmumu müzesinde gece bekçisi olarak işe başlar. Tek kuralı vardır: her turda figürleri yüksek sesle saymak. İkinci gece sayı bir fazla çıkar.
paragraphs: On Kerem's first night at the Marlowe Wax Museum, there were twelve figures. On his second night, there were thirteen.

He had taken the job because he needed money, and because the advertisement had made him smile. NIGHT GUARD WANTED. QUIET WORK. MUST BE GOOD AT COUNTING. The owner, Mrs. Quill, was a small woman with grey hair and very bright eyes. She gave him a torch, a ring of keys and a sheet of rules.
"Three rounds every night," she said. "At ten, at one and at four. You walk through every room and you count the figures. Out loud, Mr. Aydın. Always out loud."
"Why out loud?" Kerem asked.
"Because the building likes to hear a living voice."
Kerem laughed. Mrs. Quill did not.
"And how many figures are there?" he asked.
"Twelve. There have always been twelve." She looked past him, at the dark door of the first room. "The last guard left very suddenly. I hope you will be more sensible."

The museum stood at the end of Harbour Road, in a seaside town that was empty in winter. Inside, twelve wax figures waited in six cold rooms: a pirate captain, a queen in a green dress, a boxer, a singer in a silver dress, two little girls with a ball, and others. In the light of the torch their glass eyes shone, and their faces looked almost alive.

On the first night, Kerem felt silly. He walked from room to room and counted in a loud, nervous voice. "One. Two. Three." His voice sounded small in the big dark halls. At ten o'clock, he counted twelve. At one, twelve. At four, twelve. Nothing happened. He went home at seven and slept like a stone.

On the second night, everything was the same until four o'clock. The last room on his round was called Victorian Street. It was a small room with a lamp-post and a wooden bench. Kerem shone his torch on the bench, and a man was sitting there.
He wore a grey jacket. His hat lay on his knees. His head was bent, as if he was very tired or very sad.
"Thirteen," Kerem said, before he could stop himself.

The man did not move. Kerem's heart was beating hard. He made himself walk closer. The man's hands were pale and perfect, and his shoes were clean. It's only a wax figure, he told himself. Someone has put it here as a joke. But Mrs. Quill had said twelve. And there was something strange about the grey jacket. It had a small silver badge on the chest. Kerem looked down at his own jacket. It had the same badge.

One of the rules said: Never touch the figures. So he took out his phone and took a photograph instead. Then he looked at the screen. It showed a wooden bench, a lamp-post, and nothing else. The bench was empty.
He looked up. The man was sitting there, head bent, hat on his knees. He looked down at the phone. Empty bench. Up. Man. Down. Nothing.
Kerem finished the round very fast. "Ten, eleven, twelve!" he shouted at the empty halls, and he did not say thirteen again.
At seven, Mrs. Quill arrived with a bag of warm bread. Kerem tried to sound calm. "There's a man on the bench in Victorian Street," he said. "A thirteenth figure."
Mrs. Quill stopped with her hand on the kettle. For a moment, her bright eyes were not friendly at all. "Did you count him?" she asked.
"I said the number. Just once."
"That was not clever." Then she smiled again, as if nothing had happened. "There are twelve figures, Mr. Aydın. Tired people see strange things. Go home and sleep."

But Kerem did not go home. He went to the staff room and opened the locker with the name DUNN on it. Inside were a brown coat, a pair of gloves, a packet of biscuits that had gone green, and a phone. The battery was dead, so he plugged the phone into the wall. The screen lit up. It showed a photograph of a thin man with a brown moustache, smiling beside an old woman. Under the picture it said: 41 missed calls from Mum. The last one was three weeks old.
There was also a piece of paper in the locker, folded very small. The writing was shaky, as if the writer had been in a hurry.
COUNT OUT LOUD. EVERY ROUND. IF YOU HEAR IT COUNT AFTER YOU, DO NOT STOP AT TWELVE. — T. Dunn
Kerem read it three times. He should leave this job, he knew that. But the rent was due on Friday, and there were forty-one calls on that phone that nobody had answered.

On the third night, the man was no longer on the bench. Kerem found him in the main hall, standing under the big clock. This time his head was lifted, and his eyes were closed. Kerem recognized the thin face and the brown moustache. He pointed his torch at the floor and walked past very quickly, counting loudly. And behind him, in the empty dark, a voice began to count too.
It was a thin whisper, like paper moving. It was always half a second late.
"One," said Kerem.
"...one," whispered the dark.
"Two."

He did not turn around. He counted all twelve figures with the whisper following him from room to room. When he said "Twelve," the whisper said "...twelve," and then it waited. Kerem could hear it waiting. He ran back to the guard room, locked the door and sat with his back against it until the windows turned grey.

On the fourth night, he almost stayed at home. But he thought about the phone and the forty-one calls. If he stayed at home, who would ever help Mr. Dunn? At ten o'clock he was at the door with his torch.
At four o'clock exactly, all the lights in the building went out.
The dark was complete. The torch made a small yellow circle on the floor, and the circle was shaking. "One," Kerem said. His voice was thin as a thread.
"...one," said the whisper, very close behind him.
He kept walking. "Two."

The steps behind him were slow and heavy, like the steps of a man who has forgotten how to walk. The air grew colder. Kerem's fingers felt stiff on the torch, and white, like candles. He counted the pirate captain, whose glass eyes seemed to follow him. He counted the queen, the boxer, the singer in her silver dress. At last he reached the final room and said, "Twelve."
"...twelve."
Then there was silence.

Kerem stood very still. The silence felt like a question. Behind him, the whisper did not go on. It waited, as it had waited every night, for someone to say the next number. And he thought about the shaky note in his pocket. DO NOT STOP AT TWELVE. Every guard before him had counted twelve, said "good," and gone home. Nobody had ever counted the one who followed them.

His mouth was dry. Slowly, he turned round and lifted the torch. The man in the grey jacket stood less than a metre away. His eyes were open now. They were brown, and they were wet. They did not look like glass at all.
"Thirteen," Kerem said. His voice shook, but he went on. "Thirteen. Mr. Tom Dunn, night guard of the Marlowe Wax Museum."

For a long moment, nothing happened. Then the man's shoulders dropped, as if someone had taken a heavy bag from them. He breathed out, a long, long breath that smelled of old candles. "Thank you," he whispered, and this time his voice was not half a second late. It was only a voice. Then the torch flickered, and there was nobody in front of Kerem. A grey hat lay on the floor.
All the lights came back on at once. In every room, the clocks began to tick.

At six, Mrs. Quill opened the front door. She walked through the museum without a word, her lips moving as she counted silently. In Victorian Street she stopped. The bench was empty. She stood looking at it for a long time.

"You counted him," she said at last. She did not sound angry. She sounded like a woman who had lost something valuable. "Do you know how much a night guard costs, Mr. Aydın? Salary, holidays, sick days. And for three weeks I had one who never asked for anything."
Kerem put the keys and the torch on the table. Then he took the phone out of his pocket. "I think Mr. Dunn's mother wants to hear from him," he said. "I'll find her."
Mrs. Quill looked at the phone, and for a moment Kerem thought she would say no. Instead, she pushed an envelope across the table. "Your wages," she said. "Count them, if you like."
Kerem did not count them. He did not want to count anything ever again.

There were twelve old street lamps along Harbour Road. He knew, because he had counted them on his first day, the way he now counted everything. He counted them again as he walked home, out loud, and his voice sounded strong in the empty morning. Eleven. Twelve.
At the end of the road, there was a thirteenth lamp.

It had not been there before. Under its yellow light stood a thin man with a brown moustache. He did not look like wax now. He looked like a man who was going home at last. He lifted one hand, slowly, like someone waving across a wide river.
Kerem lifted his hand too.

Then the lamp went out, and so did the man. Kerem looked at the road for a long time. There were only twelve lamps. He put his hand in his pocket, felt the phone, and began to walk faster. Somebody's mother had been waiting for three weeks.

phrases.tr: kendini yaklaşmaya zorladı (make oneself do: kendini zorlamak)

quiz.q: What is Mrs. Quill's most important rule for the night guard?
options: Never talk to visitors
Touch every figure once
Count the figures out loud on every round
Stay in the guard room all night
quiz.explainTr: Mrs. Quill, her turda figürlerin yüksek sesle sayılmasını ister: 'Out loud, Mr. Aydın. Always out loud.'

quiz.q: What does Kerem see when he takes a photograph of the bench?
options: A man in a grey jacket
An empty bench
Mrs. Quill
A pirate captain
quiz.explainTr: Gözle bankta bir adam görür ama telefondaki fotoğrafta bank bomboştur.

quiz.q: Why does Kerem keep going to work after he finds Mr. Dunn's phone?
options: He wants to see the ghost again
Mrs. Quill offers him more money
He is not afraid of ghosts
He thinks about the unanswered calls from Dunn's mother
quiz.explainTr: Kerem, telefonda cevapsız kalan 41 aramayı düşünür ve işe gitmeye devam eder.

quiz.q: What does Kerem do that helps the thirteenth figure?
options: He counts him and says his name
He breaks the clock
He runs out of the building
He turns off the lights
quiz.explainTr: Kerem 'Thirteen. Mr. Tom Dunn' diyerek onu sayar ve ismini söyler; Dunn rahatlar.

quiz.q: What is strange about the last street lamp on Harbour Road?
options: It is much brighter than the others
It was not there before
It is broken
It is the first lamp Kerem sees
quiz.explainTr: Yolda her zaman on iki lamba vardır; on üçüncü lamba daha önce orada değildi.
